name: Projects funded from a growing pot
brief:
A start-up fund holds `capital` pounds. Each project in `projects` is `[need, profit]`: it can start only when the fund holds at least `need`, and when it finishes the fund gains `profit`, which is never negative. Projects run one at a time, each at most once, and the fund may run at most `k` of them. Return the largest amount the fund can end with.

Write `funded_projects(capital, k, projects)`.

Example. For `capital = 1`, `k = 2` and `projects = [[4, 6], [1, 2], [0, 3], [3, 1]]`, two projects are open at the start, and the profit of 3 takes the fund to 4. That opens `[4, 6]`, so the answer is `10`.
constraints: At most $100{,}000$ projects and $0 \le k \le 100{,}000$; needs and profits are whole numbers from 0 to $10^9$.
$O((n + k) \log n)$ time is the target. Scanning every project for each of `k` choices is $O(nk)$, too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Sort the projects by `need`. Before each choice, move every project the fund can now afford into a max-heap of profits; then take the top. Stop early when the heap is empty.

examples.note: Taking the profit of 3 first opens the project that needs 4.
Nothing is affordable at the start, so the fund stays at 5.

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method scans every unused project before each choice, which is $O(nk)$ and runs out of time on the large tests. The step to the target is to sort by need and keep the affordable profits in a max-heap, so each project enters it once.
notes: Profits never shrink the fund, so taking the biggest affordable profit each time is never worse.
Taking the cheapest project, or the best project from the start only, misses projects the growing fund unlocks.
Sorting is $O(n \log n)$ and each project enters and leaves the heap once, so the work is $O((n + k) \log n)$.

planted.slip: A strict `<` refuses a project whose need equals the fund exactly.
Taking the cheapest projects first spends the `k` choices on small profits.
Choosing only among projects affordable at the start ignores what the growing fund unlocks.
